claim: Google's revenue share payment to Apple in 2022 was an estimated $20 billion (worldwide queries), nearly double the 2020 payment, which was then equivalent to 17.5% of Apple's operating profit.
stance_target: dollar magnitude of Google TAC to Apple -- gold-standard court trial testimony figure
scope_conditions: US v. Google liability trial, FOF P299, testimony of Eddy Cue (Tr. 2492-93) and Michael Whinston
quoted_support: In 2022, Google's revenue share payment to Apple was an estimated $20 billion (worldwide queries). This is nearly double the payment made in 2020, which was then equivalent to 17.5% of Apple's operating profit.

claim: Google's 2022 ISA payment to Apple exceeded the combined total of all of Google's other revenue-share payments to every other distribution partner, and was approximately double that combined value.
stance_target: relative concentration of Google TAC exposure in the Apple relationship specifically
scope_conditions: US v. Google liability trial, testimony of Michael Whinston discussing UPXD104
quoted_support: Google's 2022 payment under the ISA is more than all of its other revenue share payments combined and is approximately double that combined value.

claim: The exact percentage of ad revenue Google pays Apple under the ISA is redacted even in the public court record; only the resulting dollar figure and the 2020 ratio to Apple's operating profit survived redaction.
stance_target: confirms the query's premise that Apple/Google do not disclose the TAC line item and that even court discovery only partially surfaces it
scope_conditions: US v. Google liability opinion, public redacted version
quoted_support: In return for exclusive and non-exclusive default placements (i.e., user-downloaded Chrome and Safari default bookmarks), Google pays Apple __% of its net ad revenue, which amounted to $20 billion in 2022.

claim: In 2021, Google spent $26.3 billion in traffic acquisition costs across all distribution partners, four times more than the company's other search-related costs combined including R&D.
stance_target: company-wide dollar magnitude of Google TAC (all partners, not Apple alone)
scope_conditions: US v. Google liability opinion, FOF P289
quoted_support: In 2021, Google spent $26.3 billion in traffic acquisition costs -- the revenue share paid to its partners -- which is four times more than the company's other search-related costs combined, including research and development.

claim: Google's internal 'Alice in Wonderland' analysis projected Microsoft would need to offer Apple over 100% revenue share to win the default; Microsoft did in fact offer Apple 100% revenue share plus guarantees, and Apple's executives still testified that Bing was never a realistic option to replace Google, because of a product quality gap rather than price.
stance_target: alternative bidders (Microsoft/Bing) set a meaningful competitive floor under Apple's Google TAC exposure
scope_conditions: US v. Google liability trial, FOF P323-328
quoted_support: Google's "Alice in Wonderland" analysis projected that Microsoft would have to offer Apple over 100% revenue share to compete, FOF P328, and this study turned out to be wholly accurate. Microsoft did offer Apple 100% revenue share plus guarantees, but Apple's executives testified that Bing was never a realistic option to replace Google.
time_period: as found in Aug 2024 liability opinion

claim: Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified that Google took into account that Apple had no viable alternative to Google search, which is why Google did not pay Apple the higher revenue share Apple wanted.
stance_target: genuine price competition for the Apple default exists under current market structure
scope_conditions: US v. Google liability trial testimony, Tr. 7772-7773 (Pichai)
quoted_support: Even Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified that Google took "into account" that Apple had no other viable option "which was why [it] didn't pay the share Apple wanted."
time_period: as found in Aug 2024 liability opinion

claim: Apple has built substantial internal search infrastructure and technology (hiring ex-Google-Search head John Giannandrea in 2018) and both Apple and Google understand Apple could develop its own GSE to replace Google as the Safari default, but Apple has decided not to do so, partly due to the revenue-share loss and partly due to billions in additional required investment, ad-platform build-out, and brand/product risk.
stance_target: Apple's own strategic optionality to internalize search rather than depend on Google TAC
scope_conditions: US v. Google liability opinion, FOF P300-302
quoted_support: Both Apple and Google understand that Apple could develop its own GSE to replace Google as the default in Safari. Apple has decided not to do so thus far. ... it would have to commit billions more to build and maintain a fully functioning GSE. It also would need to develop an ad platform to monetize searches. Critically, Apple would have to be willing to put its brand reputation -- and possibly device sales -- at stake if it were to produce an inferior or unpopular product.
time_period: 2018 onward, as found in Aug 2024 liability opinion

claim: Over 65% of searches on all Apple devices go through the Safari default, and Google pays Apple revenue share even on Chrome queries despite Apple not preloading Chrome.
stance_target: concentration of Apple's dependence on the Safari default channel
scope_conditions: US v. Google liability opinion, FOF P74-75, P296
quoted_support: Over 65% of searches on all Apple devices go through the Safari default. FOF P296.
time_period: as found in Aug 2024 liability opinion
